title: Josephine Cochrane and the invention of the dishwasher: chipped china, the 1886 patent, and the 1893 World's Fair

facts.text: Josephine Cochrane was born in 1839 in Ashtabula County, Ohio, and died in 1913 in Chicago at age 74.
Her father was a civil engineer, and an earlier relative, John Fitch, was a steamboat inventor.
facts.note: Lemelson-MIT 說 John Fitch 是曾祖父，USPTO 說是外祖父；題目不用這個細節

facts.text: Cochrane and her husband William lived in Shelbyville, Illinois, and often entertained guests; servants did much of the housework, including washing dishes.
Her fine china, said to be very old family dishes, often got chipped when it was washed by hand.
Her husband died in 1883 and left her about $1,500 along with growing debts, which pushed her to make her machine work and sell it.
She built the first working model in 1886 in a shed behind her home, with the help of a mechanic named George Butters.
She measured her dishes and made wire compartments shaped to fit plates, cups, and saucers.
The compartments sat inside a wheel that lay flat in a copper boiler; a motor turned the wheel while hot soapy water sprayed up over the dishes.
Earlier dishwashing machines relied on scrubbers or on pouring boiling water over dishes; hers cleaned with water pressure and held the dishes in fitted racks.
She applied for a patent on December 31, 1885, and received U.S. patent No. 355,139 for a dish washing machine in late December 1886.
Her machines first sold to businesses such as hotels and restaurants rather than to families.
Her first order came in 1887 from the Palmer House, a hotel in Chicago.
Families were put off by the price, about $350 for a home model, and by the large amount of hot water the machine needed.
Some homemakers also disliked the soapy film the machine left on dishes.
Hospitals and colleges also bought her machines because they needed very clean dishes.
At the 1893 World's Fair in Chicago, nine of her machines were used in the fair's restaurants.
Judges at the 1893 fair gave her machine the top prize for its mechanical construction and durability, and orders grew afterward.
A large model shown at the fair could wash and dry 240 dishes in two minutes.
Around 1898 she opened her own factory; her company was bought by Hobart in 1926 and its dishwashers were sold under the KitchenAid name.
Whirlpool bought KitchenAid in 1986, so her company eventually became part of Whirlpool.
Dishwashers became common in homes only in the 1950s and 1960s, decades after Cochrane died.
facts.note: Lemelson-MIT 說 1950 年代普及率大增，USPTO 說 1960 年代成為常見家電

facts.text: Cochrane was added to the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2006.

notes: 姓氏在專利上寫 Cochran，其他資料多寫 Cochrane；選文用 Cochrane。專利號、申請日與 1893 年博覽會的事實以 USPTO 為準。
